Choosing a model is the first real decision in an IRT analysis, and the one
a committee or a technical advisory panel asks about first. The flowchart
below starts from what a single item score looks like, asks one or two
questions, and ends at a model and the `itemtype` that fits it in mirt.

## Not sure? Let the data compare

If the questions do not settle it, fit the usual candidates and compare
them. `select_model()` picks the candidates from the data (Rasch, 2PL and
3PL for 0/1 items; partial credit, generalized partial credit and graded for
ordered items), ranks them by BIC, runs likelihood-ratio tests between
nested models, and explains its pick:

```{r}
library(mirtverse)
sel <- select_model(expand.table(LSAT7))
sel            # comparison table and a plain-language explanation
mod <- sel$best
interpret(mod)
```

The statistics are only half of the decision. The purpose of the test
matters too: A Rasch model can be the right choice even when a 2PL fits a
little better, because it keeps the sum score as the whole story.

## Right or wrong (0/1) items

**Could low scorers guess the right answer?** On multiple-choice items with
a few options, they often can. The 3PL adds a lower asymptote for guessing,
but it needs large samples (about 1,000 people or more) to estimate well.

```{r}
data <- expand.table(LSAT7)
mod3 <- mirt(data, 1, itemtype = "3PL")
```

**Should every item count the same in the score?** If yes, use the Rasch
model: All items share one slope, the sum score carries all the information
about ability, and it works with smaller samples (from about 100 people). If
items should be allowed to discriminate differently, use the 2PL (aim for
about 500 people or more).

```{r}
mod1 <- mirt(data, 1, itemtype = "Rasch")
mod2 <- mirt(data, 1, itemtype = "2PL")
anova(mod1, mod2)   # does the extra slope per item pay off?
gg_trace(mod2)
```

## Ordered categories

**Are points earned step by step on a rubric?** For constructed responses
and tasks scored 0, 1, 2 and so on, the generalized partial credit model
treats each score as a step. Its Rasch version, the partial credit model, is
`itemtype = "Rasch"` in mirt when items have more than two categories.

```{r}
mod_gpcm <- mirt(Science, 1, itemtype = "gpcm")
mod_pcm  <- mirt(Science, 1, itemtype = "Rasch")
```

**Same rating scale on every item, and a Rasch model wanted?** The rating
scale model gives all items the same set of thresholds, which makes it the
most compact choice. Otherwise, the graded response model is the usual pick
for Likert scales.

```{r}
mod_rsm <- mirt(Science, 1, itemtype = "rsm")
mod_grm <- mirt(Science, 1, itemtype = "graded")
gg_trace(mod_grm)
```

## Unordered options

When you care about which wrong option a person chose, keep the raw
responses and fit the nominal response model. It shows which distractors
attract lower-ability test takers and which ones do not work. `SAT12` stores
the raw option chosen (1 to 5) for 32 items.

```{r}
raw <- SAT12
raw[raw == 8] <- NA            # 8 marks an omitted item
mod_nom <- mirt(raw, 1, itemtype = "nominal")
gg_trace(mod_nom, items = 1:4)
```

## Agree only if close (unfolding)

Some attitude statements describe a middle position, such as "Social media
is fine in moderation". People on both extremes disagree
with it, for opposite reasons. Ideal-point (unfolding) models handle this,
and the generalized graded unfolding model (GGUM) is available in mirt:

```{r}
mod_ggum <- mirt(Science, 1, itemtype = "ggum")
```

## Then think about the structure

Each of these questions adds one argument or one function to the model you
picked above.

| Question | What to do | Learn more |
|---|---|---|
| More than one trait? | Check local dependence with `gg_q3(mod)`, then fit `mirt(data, 2)` or a confirmatory `mirt.model()` | [Glossary: Dimensionality](glossary.html#dimensionality) |
| Items in clusters (testlets, shared passages)? | A general factor plus specific factors with `bfactor(data, specific)` | `?bfactor` |
| Groups to compare? | Screen items with `dif(mod, group)`, then put groups on one scale with `multipleGroup()` | [Lab 3: DIF](teaching-labs.html) |
| Item features explain difficulty? | Explanatory IRT (LLTM) with `predict_difficulty()`, the [eirm](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=eirm) package or `mixedmirt()` | [Book: Item text](../book/item-text.html) |
| Response times too? | Model speed together with ability with `fit_rt(mod, rt)` | [Response times](../articles/response-times.html) |
| Classes rather than a continuum? | Mastery groups or latent classes with `mdirt(data, 2)` | `?mdirt` |

## Before you trust the model

Whatever path you took, check the result before you report it:

```{r}
glance(mod)       # overall fit: M2, RMSEA, CFI, SRMSR
gg_itemfit(mod)   # items that misfit
gg_trace(mod)     # curves that look strange
interpret(mod)    # a plain-language summary
```

A simpler model that fits is easier to explain. Move to a richer one only
when the fit checks or the purpose of the test call for it. The
[thesis kit](thesis-kit.html) turns these checks into a Methods paragraph.

## A note on sample sizes

The sample sizes on the poster are rough rules of thumb drawn from the IRT
literature, not guarantees. More items, well-targeted items and simpler
models all need fewer people; the 3PL and the nominal model need the most.
When in doubt, simulate: `simdata()` in mirt can show how well your planned
sample recovers the parameters.
